name: Regional Dress
description: Iran’s regional dress traditions differ in garment construction, textiles, embroidery, and ways of combining layers. Documented examples from the Caspian coast, southeastern Iran, and the Persian Gulf show both local distinctions and changes in materials and manufacture.

seo.title: Regional Dress in Iran: Garments, Materials and Local Variation
seo.description: Explore documented dress traditions from Gilan, Baluchistan and the Persian Gulf, with attention to construction, embroidery and historical context.

content.heading: Reading clothing through place and time
content.content:
Regional dress becomes easier to understand when an outfit is treated as a combination of garments rather than a single national costume. The Textile Research Centre in Leiden documents shirts, trousers, skirts, shawls, waistcoats, and head coverings whose combinations differ across Iran. Its exhibition draws largely on garments collected during research between 1999 and 2003; these are valuable records of particular places and periods, rather than a survey of what everyone wears today. [s1]

The examples below therefore describe documented traditions. They should not be used to identify a person’s ethnicity from appearance or to assume that a photographed ceremonial outfit represents ordinary daily clothing.

content.heading: Gilan: cloth, layers, and working garments
content.content:
Along the southern Caspian coast, Gilan’s clothing traditions combine locally produced cloth with garments of different cuts. The Leiden collection describes women’s gathered skirts worn over trousers, with a tunic and waistcoat above. It records variation within Gilan itself: skirts could be shorter in eastern districts and longer in the west. Waistcoats also differed between everyday and special-occasion use. These distinctions belong to the exhibition’s historical frame, not a fixed dress code for present-day residents. [s2]

Ethnologist Christian Bromberger identifies *shal*, a coarse wool cloth, and *chadershab*, a rectangular cloth tied around the waist, as characteristic Caspian elements. In eastern Gilan, chadershab could be woven from silk-floss strips. He specifically cautions that the checked cloth associated with Qasemabad should not be treated as typical of the entire region. His account, published in 1992, is particularly useful for understanding local variation and the relationship between textile production and clothing. [s3]

content.heading: Baluch and Gulf examples
content.content:
For southeastern Iran, the Leiden exhibition describes a Baluch woman’s ensemble of trousers, a dress called *pashk*, and a large shawl or head covering called *sarig*. Embroidery appears in defined areas, including the chest, pocket, and cuffs. The exhibition records both hand stitching and the increasing use of machine embroidery; it also notes that embroidered panels could be removed from worn garments and attached to new ones. [s1]

Along the Persian Gulf in Hormozgan, the same exhibition highlights women’s decorated trouser cuffs beneath a dress. Its account distinguishes earlier locality-associated cuff patterns from later choices based on personal preference. Such examples show why a motif cannot always be read as an unchanging geographical label. [s1]

content.heading: What a garment can reveal
content.content:
A useful first question is how an outfit was made: which cloth was woven locally, which decoration was added afterward, and which pieces were layered together? Caspian shal and Baluch embroidery illustrate different kinds of knowledge—making the fabric itself and working decoration onto garments. Both matter to the finished ensemble. [s1][s3]

A careful description also states where and when an example was documented. That small discipline preserves the richness of regional dress while leaving room for individual choice and historical change.

name: Local Textile Weaving
description: Local textile weaving in Iran includes fabrics made for clothing, furnishings, and floor coverings using different fibers and loom structures. Historical workshop evidence and surviving objects reveal connections between Caspian materials, urban silk production, cotton weaving, and the reuse of valuable cloth.

seo.title: Local Textile Weaving in Iran: Silk, Termeh and Cotton Cloth
seo.description: Understand Iranian woven textiles through fibers, loom techniques, regional production and documented examples of silk, termeh and cotton zilu.

content.heading: Start with the structure
content.content:
A woven textile is formed by interlacing two sets of threads: the warp, held under tension on the loom, and the weft, worked across it. Changing their arrangement changes the fabric’s surface and the possibilities for pattern. The Metropolitan Museum of Art’s account of Safavid textiles distinguishes complex lampas fabrics from velvets, whose raised pile could cover the surface or alternate with flatter areas. The Safavids were the dynasty that ruled Iran during the sixteenth and early eighteenth centuries. [s1]

These distinctions help separate material from technique. Silk names a fiber; velvet describes a fabric structure. An elaborate pattern need not have been embroidered onto finished cloth: it could have been created during weaving itself. [s1]

content.heading: Regional production formed connected networks
content.content:
The Met’s historical synthesis describes a textile economy linking small silk-producing farms in the Caspian region with urban workshops. Court production existed alongside private enterprises: Yazd and Kashan remained important producers of luxury silks for markets within and beyond Iran. This was a connected economy rather than a collection of isolated village crafts. [s1]

Local cloth also answered different practical needs. Bromberger’s account of Caspian clothing describes *shal*, a coarse plain-woven sheep’s-wool fabric scrubbed in soapy water after weaving. In eastern Gilan, silk-floss strips were woven on pedal looms to make *chadershab*, cloth used around the waist and for carrying infants. These examples connect weaving to particular garments and tasks rather than to luxury alone. [s2]

content.heading: Termeh: a fabric with more than one life
content.content:
A textile in the Smithsonian’s National Museum of Asian Art provides a closely documented example of *termeh*, a patterned cloth associated with prestigious clothing in Qajar Iran. The museum dates this silk-and-wool example to approximately 1875–1900 and attributes it probably to Yazd. Both qualifications matter: neither an exact production year nor a certain workshop location is established. [s3]

The museum interprets its present form as a table cover assembled from fragments of a former robe of honor—a garment bestowed by a ruler. Its history therefore includes cutting, rearranging, and reuse, not simply manufacture. The museum also describes the later mechanization of termeh production and its broader use for covers. A traditional textile name does not, by itself, establish that a modern example was handwoven. [s3]

content.heading: Cotton weaving and careful comparison
content.content:
Silk should not overshadow cotton. A comparative study by Ashkan Rahmani and Majid Reza Moghanipoor examines Iranian *zilu*, a flatwoven covering associated with desert cities including Meybod, Yazd, and Kashan. It describes cotton warp and weft, frequently in contrasting colors, and distinguishes the Iranian structure from textiles called by related names in Anatolia and the Caucasus. [s4]

The practical lesson is to ask several questions together: What is the fiber? How was the cloth woven? Where is its origin documented? What was it used for? Those questions reveal more than treating every patterned textile as the same kind of “Persian fabric.” [s1][s3][s4]

name: Kilim & Jajim
description: Kilim, commonly called gelim in Persian, and jajim belong to Iran’s flatwoven textile traditions but differ in how their visible surfaces are formed. Their structures, regional variations, and documented household uses offer a way to understand textiles beyond the category of knotted carpets.

seo.title: Kilim and Jajim in Iran: Flatweave Structures and Uses
seo.description: Learn how Iranian kilim and jajim differ, how weaving shapes their patterns, and how documented examples served households and mobile communities.

content.heading: Two ways of making a flatwoven surface
content.content:
Kilim and jajim are useful starting points for understanding textiles whose designs are built into a flatwoven surface. *Gelim* is the Persian term commonly used for the tapestry-woven textiles also known as kilims. In tapestry weaving, colored wefts—the threads worked across the loom—are packed closely enough to conceal the supporting warp. Different colors can be worked only where the pattern requires them. [s1]

Jajim is identified in Iranian textile terminology with a warp-faced structure: the lengthwise threads dominate the visible surface. The contrast concerns the organization of the fabric, not simply its color or whether it has stripes. A comparative weaving study also warns that the name jajim can cover different structures in neighboring regions. Terminology needs a geographical context. [s2]

content.heading: How technique shapes kilim design
content.content:
In slit-tapestry kilims, adjacent areas of color turn back around separate warp threads, leaving openings where they meet. Long openings weaken the fabric, encouraging stepped or interrupted boundaries. Other tapestry methods join neighboring colors and allow different effects. Geometric design is therefore partly a response to construction, although skilled weavers can also achieve curved forms. [s1]

Regional comparisons reveal further differences. Sumru Belger Krody’s survey highlights finely woven Sanandaj examples and the double-interlocked structures of Bakhtiari textiles. It also notes that many southern gelims passed through the market at Shiraz. A market name and a place of manufacture are not necessarily identical, and the same broad label can conceal considerable technical variation. [s1]

content.heading: Jajim: narrow weaving, wider cloth
content.content:
A documented jajim attributed to Birjand in eastern Iran illustrates how a large textile could be assembled from narrow woven strips. Saffronart’s catalogue describes strips joined along their finished side edges, or selvedges, and associates the narrow format with maintaining even tension during weaving. The catalogued piece combines repeated colored bands with smaller white designs. [s3]

The same catalogue describes jajim used as floor spreads, bedding covers, blankets, hangings, and partitions within tents. These are recorded uses, not a rule governing every example. The catalogued textile is dated approximately to 1930 and was acquired by collector Jasleen Dhamija in Birjand in December 1970. Those are separate claims about manufacture and collecting history; neither date should be substituted for the other. As an auction description, the attribution merits more caution than a documented maker’s record. [s3]

content.heading: Compare structure before labels
content.content:
When comparing examples, begin with what the textile actually shows: which threads form the surface, how neighboring colors meet, and whether separate strips have been joined. Then consider the recorded place, date, and use. The scholarly distinction between warp-faced jajim and tapestry-woven gelim provides a stronger basis for description than appearance alone. [s1][s2]

An attractive stripe or repeated motif cannot independently establish age, community, or place of manufacture. Those identifications require provenance and technical examination. Read together, structure and documentation reveal these textiles as designed household objects, rather than interchangeable decorative rugs.
